pages.title: Clynelish distillery - Wikipedia
pages.description: Encyclopedia entry on Clynelish distillery near Brora and the original Clynelish beside it.
pages.text:
Clynelish distillery is a distillery near Brora, Sutherland, in the Highlands of Scotland. Owner: Diageo. Founded: 1967. Status: Operational. Water source: Clynemilton burn. No. of stills: 3 wash stills, 3 spirit stills. Capacity: 4,800,000 litres.

History
The original Clynelish distillery was built in 1819, next to the present Clynelish distillery, which was built in 1967. In its first years, 1820 to 1822, it made about 12,000 gallons (about 54,000 litres) a year. It passed from owner to owner and was expanded around 1896 to about 580,000 litres, when an extra warehouse was added.

In the 1960s more and more Clynelish spirit went into blends, and demand was booming, so in 1967 the current distillery was built. For a while the two ran side by side as Clynelish A and Clynelish B, to make sure the taste was right in the new plant, and then the older distillery was closed.

Later, when Caol Ila faced a drought and closed for a year for rebuilding, Johnnie Walker was short of peated whisky. So Clynelish reopened the original distillery in May 1969 under the name Brora Distillery, and it ran until July 1983. Brora's last release of the original spirit was a 40 year old bi-centenary bottling of 1819 bottles.

Clynelish has long been linked with Johnnie Walker and has been called the backbone of Gold Label Reserve.

Visitor centre
As part of Diageo's £185 million investment in tourism in Scotland, the Clynelish visitor centre opened in April 2021, at a reported cost of £5M. In early 2026 Diageo confirmed it would close the centre, citing low visitor numbers and difficulty finding staff.

pages.title: Clynelish | Scotch Whisky
pages.description: Whiskypedia entry on Clynelish with its history, timeline, facts and owners.
pages.text:
Clynelish. Distillery & brand. Region: Highland. Distillery Status: Working. Clynelish makes an unusual 'waxy' new make spirit, and its spirit stills are larger than its wash stills.

History
Clynelish was one of the 'Clearance' distilleries of the early 19th century. The Duke of Sutherland, who moved tenant farmers off their land, set up businesses in Brora to employ them, including a distillery he called Clynelish. It was not a success at first and only built a reputation in 1896, when the blenders Ainslie & Heilbron bought it in partnership with John Risk, who became the outright owner in 1912. When John Walker & Sons was folded into DCL in 1925, Clynelish came too. It closed in the 1930s but made small amounts of spirit during the Second World War.

Like many DCL distilleries, it got a new plant with six stills, built beside the original distillery in 1968; until then Clynelish had only one pair of stills. The old plant was mothballed for a year before running alongside as 'Clynelish B'. It was renamed Brora in 1969, when it began making a heavily peated spirit for blending, after a drought on Islay and then the rebuilding of Caol Ila. Brora's heavily peated years lasted until 1973, and it finally closed in 1983. The original distillery is being rebuilt.

In 2014 Diageo announced a £30m expansion of Clynelish, but the plan has since been postponed. In 2018 it announced £150m for tourism, including a better visitor centre at Clynelish.

Timeline
1819 Clynelish founded by the first Duke of Sutherland
1827 Its first licensed distiller, James Harper, goes bankrupt; John Matheson takes control
1846 The distillery is sold to George Lawson & Sons
1896 James Ainslie & Heilbron acquire Clynelish
1912 DCL takes over the distillery with James Risk
1931 Clynelish is mothballed
1960 Production resumes
1967 A second distillery, also named Clynelish, is built next door. A year later, the original distillery is mothballed
1969 The original distillery is reopened as Brora
1983 Brora is closed
2002 Clynelish 14 Year Old is launched
2014 Diageo announces a £30m investment to expand Clynelish
2017 Diageo announces plans to reopen Brora (and Port Ellen on Islay)
2018 Clynelish's visitor centre is to get a comprehensive upgrade

Facts
Heat source: Steam. Stills: 6. Washbacks: 10 (8 wood, 2 steel). Mash tun: Lauter. Fermentation time: at least 55 hours. Water source: Clynemilton Byrne.

Owners
Current owner: Diageo, 1997 - present. Previous owners: United Distillers, 1986 - 1997; Distillers Company Limited, 1925 - 1986; John Risk, 1896 - 1925; Ainslie & Heilbron Distillers, 1896 - 1912 (jointly with John Risk); George Lawson, 1846 - 1896; Andrew Ross, 1834 - 1846; James Harper, 1828 - 1834; John Matheson, 1827 - 1828; James Harper, 1825 - 1827; Marquis of Stafford, 1819 - 1825.

pages.title: Visit Clynelish | Whisky Distillery Tours | Malts GB
pages.description: Diageo's visitor page for Clynelish, with a short history and visitor notice.
pages.text:
Clynelish Distillery & Visitor Centre
Please note: Clynelish distillery is now closed. Our nearby The Singleton of Glen Ord Distillery is open seven days a week for tours and tastings.

Founded in 1819 by the Marquess of Stafford, the original Clynelish gave Highland tenants a market for their barley. That site closed in 1968, making way for the modern distillery across the road, while Brora rose beside it, fell quiet, and returned in 2021.

Today Clynelish is one of the Four Corners of Johnnie Walker. Its spirit, known for a light waxiness, is made with Northern Highland barley and water from the Clynemilton Burn.

FAQs
Is the Clynelish distillery open? No, the Clynelish distillery is closed to visitors at the moment.
Who owns the Clynelish distillery? Clynelish is owned by Diageo.

pages.title: Clynelish Distillery
pages.description: Difford's Guide entry on Clynelish distillery in Brora.
pages.text:
Clynelish Distillery, Brora, Sutherland. Status: Operational. Established: 1967. Capacity: 4,200,000 litres. Visitor Policy: Not generally accessible. Website: www.malts.com

One of the most northerly distilleries in Scotland, Clynelish (pronounced 'Kline-leesh') was founded in 1819. The name comes from the Gaelic for 'enclosed pasture', and the original distillery was built on farmland to employ the Duke of Sutherland's resettled tenants. The present Clynelish Distillery was built in 1967-68, and the whisky made at the original distillery was called Brora until it closed in 1983.

In January 2014 Diageo, the owner, announced plans for a £30 million expansion to double capacity at Clynelish.

Bottles: Clynelish Select Reserve, part of Diageo's 2014 Special Releases; Clynelish 14 year old.

pages.title: Clynelish Distillery to Cease Tours and Close Its Visitor Center
pages.description: Trade news on the Clynelish visitor centre closing while the distillery keeps producing.
pages.text:
Clynelish Visitor Center to Close
The distillery remains in production, owner Diageo emphasized
January 26, 2026, Jonny McCormick

On March 13th, Clynelish Distillery, the Highland home of Johnnie Walker, will close its doors to visitors, owner Diageo announced. Tours will end on February 28th. Production of Clynelish's waxy single malt will continue; it is sold as a single malt and is a key part of Diageo's blends, including Johnnie Walker Gold Label Reserve. The Clynelish Waxen Sun 18 year old was part of the Diageo Special Releases 2025.

The visitor center opened during the COVID-19 pandemic. Clynelish had fewer than 20,000 visitors in 2023, far fewer than Talisker and Oban, and low foot traffic left Diageo unable to justify its running costs.

Clynelish lies on the outskirts of Brora in the Northern Highlands, on the North Coast 500 route. Its neighbour, Brora Distillery, which reopened in 2021, stays open to visitors.

expected.notes: opened 1967: the present distillery (Wikipedia: Founded: 1967 and built in 1967; ScotchWhisky.com timeline: 1967, a second distillery also named Clynelish is built next door; Difford's Guide: Established: 1967 and built in 1967-68).

notes: This is a scope case: two distilleries have carried the Clynelish name. The 1819 site, renamed Brora in 1969, is a separate Entity, and its history (the Duke of Sutherland and the Clearances, Harper, Matheson, Ross, Lawson, Ainslie & Heilbron in 1896, John Risk in 1912, the 1931 mothballing, the 1960 restart, the heavily peated years to 1973, its 1983 closure and 2021 return) belongs on the Brora page. The writer may add a generic event for the 1969 rename of the old site to Brora where it explains the Clynelish A and Clynelish B names, but must not set this distillery's opening to 1819. Conflicts: (1) The building date. ScotchWhisky.com gives 1968 in its history and 1967 in its timeline, so it supports neither; Wikipedia says 1967 and Difford's Guide says 1967-68, so 1967 is the stated value. Malts.com says the old site closed in 1968 to make way for the new one. (2) Capacity: 4,800,000 litres (Wikipedia) against 4,200,000 litres (Difford's Guide); neither says litres of alcohol, so no capacity site fact. Optional: acquired 1986 (United Distillers) and acquired 1997 (Diageo), from the ScotchWhisky.com owners list only; the new plant was built under the Distillers Company Limited, the owner from 1925, which is not an acquisition of this site. Site facts that pages support: 3 wash stills and 3 spirit stills (Wikipedia; ScotchWhisky.com says 6 stills in all), steam heating (ScotchWhisky.com) and water from the Clynemilton Burn (Wikipedia and Malts.com). Traps: Malts.com's "Clynelish distillery is now closed" means closed to visitors; Whisky Advocate says production continues, so there is no 2026 closed event. The 2021 visitor centre and its 2026 closure are visitor details, as are the 2018 tourism plan and tour dates; the 2014 £30 million expansion was postponed and did not happen; the 14 Year Old launch, Select Reserve, Waxen Sun, Gold Label and the 40 year old bi-centenary bottling are bottle details. Peated stores the owner Diageo and the Malts.com page as website. Page texts are reviewed paraphrases of the cited pages, not copies. Generic events are allowed but never required, so these are not expected: generic 1819, the original Clynelish (today Brora) founded next door (all four pages). If kept, it must be generic, not this distillery's opening.
